summary: This document introduces a collection of common data types for the YANG data modeling language. It obsoletes RFC 6021 and has itself been replaced by RFC 9911.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a shared box of ready-made building blocks like numbers and addresses for YANG models. A newer box replaced it.

subtitle: A shared toolbox of ready-made data types for writing YANG models of counters, addresses, times and names.

tldr.problem: Every YANG module that needs a counter, an IP address or a timestamp would otherwise have to invent its own definition, leading to inconsistent models.
tldr.mechanism: Two YANG modules, ietf-yang-types and ietf-inet-types, define derived types built from YANG's built-in types, many of them matching existing SMIv2 types.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6991 obsoleted RFC 6021 by adding new types. It has itself been replaced by RFC 9911.

today: RFC 6991 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9911. It had itself obsoleted RFC 6021.

sections.title: Why Common Types
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language used to model configuration and state data manipulated by the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF). It has a small set of built-in types and ways to derive new ones. This document collects common derived types that apply to all areas of management information.

They are organized in two YANG modules. ietf-yang-types holds generally useful types, and ietf-inet-types holds definitions relevant to the Internet protocol suite. This version adds new types and obsoletes RFC 6021.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of everyone inventing their own idea of what an address or a counter is, there is one shared list.

sections.title: Relation to SMIv2 Types
sections.content:
The overview maps each YANG type to an equivalent type from the Structure of Management Information Version 2 (SMIv2), described in RFC 2578 and RFC 2579. A YANG type counts as equivalent if the two have the same set of values and equivalent semantics.

For example, counter32 matches Counter32, gauge32 matches Gauge32, timeticks matches TimeTicks, mac-address matches MacAddress and port-number matches InetPortNumber. Many types, such as uuid, ipv4-address and domain-name, have no SMIv2 equivalent. This lets people moving SNMP MIB data to YANG reuse familiar meanings.
sections.plainLanguage: Many of the new bricks are copies of bricks that an older toy system already had, so people can tell which is which.

sections.title: Core Types: ietf-yang-types
sections.content:
Counters and gauges follow SMIv2. A counter32 climbs to 4294967295 and wraps to zero, and counter64 does the same up to 18446744073709551615. The zero-based variants start at zero when created, so a reader can use the first value as a delta. A gauge32 or gauge64 can go up and down but is capped at its maximum. A default SHOULD NOT be used with counter types.

Other types cover identifiers (object-identifier, object-identifier-128, yang-identifier), time (date-and-time, timeticks and timestamp), addresses (phys-address, mac-address), and strings (xpath1.0, hex-string, uuid, dotted-quad).

The date-and-time type is a profile of ISO 8601 defined by the date-time production in RFC 3339. A time offset of -00:00 means the time zone is unknown. A timestamp holds the timeticks value at which something happened, and resets to zero when the associated timeticks wraps after 497+ days.
sections.plainLanguage: Some bricks count things that only go up, some measure things that go up and down, and some hold names, times and unique ID numbers.

sections.title: Internet Types: ietf-inet-types
sections.content:
This module defines types for the Internet protocol suite: ip-version (0 unknown, 1 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6), dscp, ipv6-flow-label, port-number, as-number, ip-address, ipv4-address, ipv6-address, the ip-prefix family, domain-name, host and uri.

The port-number type is a 16-bit value from 0 to 65535 for transport protocols such as UDP, TCP, DCCP or SCTP. Zero is reserved by IANA, and can be excluded by subtyping. The address types come in two forms: the plain ones allow a zone identifier for scoped addresses, while the -no-zone variants do not. The no-zone variants are among the types new in this version.
sections.plainLanguage: These bricks are for the internet: computer addresses, door numbers called ports, names and web links.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
This document registers two XML namespace URIs in the IETF XML registry and two modules in the YANG Module Names registry: ietf-yang-types with prefix yang, and ietf-inet-types with prefix inet.

On security, the RFC says the definitions themselves have no security impact on the Internet, but using them in concrete YANG modules might. The security considerations of the YANG specification (RFC 6020) apply here as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The bricks are harmless on their own. It is what people build with them that needs care.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 6021
sections.content: Appendix A lists the additions over RFC 6021. Four types were added to ietf-yang-types: yang-identifier, hex-string, uuid and dotted-quad. Three were added to ietf-inet-types: ip-address-no-zone, ipv4-address-no-zone and ipv6-address-no-zone. The module revision date is 2013-07-15.
sections.plainLanguage: The new box has a few more bricks than the old one.
